children: Vicor’s
stock jumped 10% in extended trading Wednesday after the power-component maker announced a licensing agreement tied to its technology for high-performance artificial intelligence processors.

The Andover, Massachusetts-based company said it granted a non-exclusive license to an unidentified original equipment manufacturer. The agreement allows the licensee to procure Vertical Power Delivery modules covered by Vicor patents from suppliers that don’t hold their own licenses.
Financial terms weren’t disclosed. Vicor also didn’t identify the OEM or provide details about the expected volume of purchases and royalty payments.
Solving AI’s ‘last inch’ problem

Vertical Power Delivery, or VPD, is designed to deliver high current at low voltage to power-hungry AI computing and networking processors. Vicor said the architecture avoids the “last inch problem” associated with conventional Lateral Power Delivery, in which electricity must travel horizontally across a circuit board to reach the processor.

That journey becomes increasingly inefficient as processors require more power. VPD places the power-delivery system vertically beneath or closer to the chip, reducing electrical losses and freeing space surrounding the processor.

Vicor said its VPD systems combine a “multi-cell converter” with a specialized power-delivery network. The technology is protected by patents resulting from a decade of research conducted by the company in the United States.
Licensing model with multiple revenue paths
Under Vicor’s licensing program, OEMs and hyperscalers can purchase certain VPD components from third-party suppliers while paying royalties for the use of Vicor’s patented technology.

Licensees also can buy Vicor-manufactured current multipliers, known as MCMs, from the company’s U.S. fabrication facilities. Vicor said those components offer greater efficiency and are thinner and easier to manage mechanically and thermally than competing approaches.
Customers that buy Vicor components for high-performance AI accelerators may qualify for substantial discounts on royalties covering more standardized VPD modules obtained from other suppliers.

The structure gives customers access to multiple suppliers while giving Vicor two potential sources of revenue: product sales and patent royalties. It also may help the company participate in AI infrastructure spending without having to manufacture every component covered by its intellectual property.

The announcement appears to validate Vicor’s effort to turn its VPD patent portfolio into a broader licensing business. The agreement suggests at least one additional OEM believes it needs access to the company’s intellectual property as AI processors migrate toward higher-density power systems.

The unnamed customer limits investors’ ability to estimate the agreement’s near-term financial impact. Still, the licensing model could become increasingly valuable if VPD gains adoption among AI-chip makers, server manufacturers and hyperscale data-center operators.

Vicor also issued what amounted to a warning for companies using similar technology without a license. It said unlicensed OEMs and hyperscalers may eventually need agreements to protect their supply chains. Supplier indemnification provisions could compensate customers for royalties or damages, Vicor said, but they couldn’t prevent potential importation bans.

That language signals that patent enforcement may be an important part of the company’s strategy. It also raises the possibility of future licensing agreements as customers seek to reduce the legal and supply-chain risks surrounding AI power systems.

The 10% after-hours gain reflects expectations that Vicor can extract more value from its power-delivery patents as AI processors consume greater amounts of electricity. The new agreement provides encouraging commercial validation, but the lack of financial terms makes its immediate contribution impossible to quantify.

Investors will likely look for additional licensees, royalty disclosures and evidence that Vicor’s component sales are growing alongside its licensing operation. If VPD becomes a standard architecture for advanced AI systems, Vicor could collect revenue both from customers using its products and from those buying compatible modules elsewhere.
